chunks.text: As an example, consider this portfolio where we have Google, Apple, Gold, and Exxon from the beginning of 2010 to the end of 2010. chunks.text: then we observed at the end the total performance. And we include here a chart for S&P 500 for comparison. Now this is a unoptimized portfolio. chunks.text: S&P 500. And observe over here the allocations to the assets. 60% goes to gold, 40% to Apple, and none to Google or Exxon. Now, one thing to emphasize here is this is looking back in time. So we're looking back historically what happened in 2010 and

chunks.text: observing at the beginning of 2010 if we knew what we knew now, how should we best allocate? So there's a question as to how much this can help our portfolio going forward. And I'll give you that answer ahead of time. Indeed, when we optimize for sharp ratio, hold that portfolio, rebalance.

chunks.text: In other words, re-optimize for sharp ratio and continue that month by month. We very often, most frequently see that that improves the performance of the portfolio versus just an equal allocation. But I do want to observe that this is computing back in time. So yes, of course, we can find a better portfolio.

chunks.text: But indeed, it helps going forward as well.
